sentences.text: Oviraptor was a small, feathered dinosaur estimated to be 1.6 to 2 meters long and weighing between 33 and 40 kilograms.
It likely had two well-developed hindlimbs ending in three functional toes with a vestigial first toe and a relatively reduced tail.
The skull of Oviraptor is deep, shortened, and has large openings, measuring approximately 17.9 centimeters in length as preserved.
The scapula of Oviraptor is slightly bowed and measures 23 centimeters in length.
The skull of the Oviraptor holotype became particularly flattened and distorted during fossilization.
A nest associated with Oviraptor preserves elongatoolithid eggs that are approximately 14 centimeters long.
Most popular paintings of Oviraptor are actually based on reconstructions of the high-crested oviraptorid now known as Citipati, not on currently recognized Oviraptor specimens.
In the book Dinotopia, James Gurney renamed the animal "Ovinutrix," meaning "egg keeper," because he did not consider it an egg predator.
In the Disney movie Dinosaur, Oviraptor is depicted stealing an Iguanodon egg from which the character Aladar hatches.
The first Oviraptor remains were found in the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia in 1923 during an expedition led by Roy Chapman Andrews.
Oviraptor fossils were discovered in 1923 at the Bayn Dzak locality (Flaming Cliffs) in the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia during the Third Central Asiatic Expedition.
The genus Oviraptor was named by Osborn in 1924.
In 1986, Rinchen Barsbold determined that two specimens previously referred to Oviraptor actually belonged to a new genus, Conchoraptor.
In 1977, Rinchen Barsbold proposed that Oviraptor's robust jaws and beak were strong enough to crush mollusk shells like clams found in its geological formation.
David K. Smith rejected the crushing jaw hypothesis in 1990, arguing that Oviraptor's jaws preserved shearing surfaces rather than a crushing mechanism.
In 1995, researchers reported lizard remains in the body cavity of a holotype Oviraptor, suggesting it was partially carnivorous.
Stig Olav K. Jansen suggested Oviraptor was omnivorous, capable of catching and tearing small prey with its beak and forelimbs.
The only Oviraptor philoceratops skeleton preserved stomach contents of a lizard, implying the species was at least partially carnivorous.
Discovery of brooding Citipati specimens with similar eggs showed the eggs belonged to Oviraptor and the type specimen likely incubated them rather than eating them.
While this discovery did not rule out eggs in Oviraptor's diet, its exact feeding strategies remain unknown.
The holotype of Oviraptor is believed to be a sexually mature individual that died while incubating a nest of eggs.
A new nesting oviraptorid specimen was described by Dong and Currie in 1996 from the Bayan Mandahu Formation.
Researchers suggested that the nesting oviraptorid specimen was caught and buried by a sandstorm while incubating its eggs.
Yang and colleagues noted that adult specimens found with nests might be laying eggs rather than incubating them, and the multi-ring clutch design prevented sufficient heat transfer to inner eggs.
An average oviraptorid nest was a gently inclined mound with eggs arranged in pairs within three to four elliptical rings.
Yang and colleagues concluded that the unique oviraptorid nesting style lacks modern analogs and may not be the best example for understanding bird reproductive evolution.
Henry Osborn originally assigned Oviraptor to the family Ornithomimidae, though this was later found to be incorrect.
Osborn placed Oviraptor with ornithomimids due to its lack of teeth.
H. F. Osborn proposed that Oviraptor's toothless beak and extended palate bones were tools for breaking eggs, but this interpretation is debated.
Oviraptor is known from the Bayn Dzak locality of the Djadokhta Formation in Mongolia, dating to the Late Cretaceous between 71 and 75 million years ago.
Oviraptor lived during the Late Cretaceous, between 75 and 71 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
Oviraptor lived from the Coniacian to the Campanian stages, between 89.8 and 72.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether a Chinese specimen from the Bayan Mandahu Formation belongs to Oviraptor, as researchers noted anatomical differences in hand proportions.
